column2: The seventh note of the scale; the closing note of choice for those who cannot stretch to the high 'do'.
The favourite note of every pub singalong, deployed whenever the words run dry.
The note without which there is no F major — and Christmas carols would lose their merriest syllable.
The third note of the scale — and, paired with a six, a famous British intelligence agency.
The note with which decorating projects, practice sessions and jealous tiffs all like to begin.
An enormous triangular comb with strings; the hardest of all instruments to carry to a friend's living-room gig.
The heaviest instrument in the world, as anyone who has ever helped a friend move house can confirm.
A giant brass pipe capable of replacing the subwoofer at any party on its own.
A brass instrument with a slide, ideal for scoring sad failures — 'wah-wah-waaah'.
The principal wind instrument of every romantic film scene and late-night jazz bar.
A musical pipe with a piercing voice; the sort of instrument schools assign to children, to the despair of parents in the audience.
A Scottish leather bag with pipes, sounding as though someone stepped on a cat — but in rhythm.
The African river that decided to make a dramatic exit and created Victoria Falls.
The celebrated Egyptian pharaoh whose long name is a crossword setter's dream for filling tricky grids.
The pharaoh who raised the world's largest property without a single mortgage.
The ancient Egyptian cliff with colossal statues, once sawn apart and moved uphill away from the rising waters.
The land of smiles, fierce tom-yam soup and eternal summer — the place one longs to fly to in the middle of a British winter.
The great water artery of South-East Asia, flowing through six countries in one journey.
The ancient capital of the Khmer empire, lost in the jungles of Cambodia.
The enormous temple complex in Cambodia, so distinguished it made it onto the national flag.
The capital of the Philippines — and a classic name for sturdy office folders.
Africa's highest point, where one may sunburn and throw a snowball in the same day.
The enigmatic mountain region people leave for in search of the meaning of life and enlightenment.
Paris's principal museum with the glass pyramid, where everyone rushes to photograph precisely one painting.
Barcelona's great unfinished work by Antoni Gaudí, under construction for longer than the Egyptian pyramids took.
The hot desert of southern Africa, home to the meerkats of Lion King fame.
One of the world's oldest deserts, its red dunes running straight into the Atlantic.
The sunken island of legend, hunted by everyone except those still hunting their keys before leaving the house.
The American national park with geysers and a slumbering supervolcano that everyone is careful not to wake.
The tiny principality with more yachts and millionaires per square metre than anywhere else.
The splendid Moorish palace in Spain, beautiful enough to make one dizzy on the staircases.
The longest river of the USA, and a state easily confused with Mississippi.
The river on which St Petersburg stands, whose drawbridges strand late-night romantics on the wrong bank.
A Philippine island famed as a surfing capital, with palm-lined beaches and laid-back vibes.
The popular resort island of the Philippines, visited to swim with whale sharks.
The shaggy highland ox that looks as though it has never made the acquaintance of a comb.
The world's largest flower; it looks like an alien and smells like a week's worth of rubbish.
A fragrant tropical blossom used in traditional garlands and heady perfumes.
The spring flower with a curled cluster, named for a youth of myth — and for television's most determined social climber.
The windowsill 'household doctor' that raises baby plants along the very edges of its leaves.
The miniature spring flower resembling a tiny bunch of blue grapes.
The optimist's flower, turning its head after the sun all day long.
A tall cereal crop with golden kernels, and the raw material behind cinema popcorn.
The noble flower whose scent is strong enough that one should never leave it in the bedroom overnight.
The physical phenomenon by which an ordinary ray of light becomes the rainbow on the cover of a certain celebrated rock album.
The device that sees aircraft in the sky — and, by the roadside, notes who is hurrying to the party a little too eagerly.
The chemical element of which we ourselves, pencil leads and diamonds are all made.
The lightest and first element of the periodic table, without which there would be no water.
The yellow element smelling of matches, volcanoes and the nether regions.
The treacherous poison of detective novels, once administered to inconvenient relatives.
The branch of physics concerned with cogs and levers — and, in a car, the gearbox for those who like to change gear themselves.
The mathematical chance that the sandwich lands butter-side down (tending, in practice, to 100%).
The sideways figure of eight; also the precise duration of a Friday afternoon at the office.
A quiet battery-driven vehicle that plugs in for power much like a smartphone.
Water in its gaseous state, without which neither the sauna nor a good iron is possible.
The doughnut-shaped figure of mathematics; a word that sounds suspiciously like the Norse god of thunder.
The transparent semi-precious stone, most often sky-blue or golden.
The violet quartz the ancients wore as a charm against hangovers — hence all those drinking cups.
The gemstone the colour of fresh olive oil or spring grass.
The variegated ornamental stone on which nature paints like an abstract artist.
The banded mineral whose cut face reveals whole landscapes.
The fossilised resin of ancient pines, in which prehistoric mosquitoes occasionally got stuck.
A world religion teaching nirvana, calm and the art of letting problems go.
The principal Buddhist festival, marking the birth, enlightenment and passing of the Buddha.
That very lady from Leonardo's painting, smiling enigmatically at every museum visitor — behind a queue one cannot fight.
The stone 'sleeping bag' of ancient rulers and mummies.
The three-headed dog guarding the entrance to the realm of the dead; also the nightclub doorman with overly strict face control.
The superpower of understanding another's feelings, and of weeping at sad films for moral support.
The powerful emotional release that follows a gripping film, a stirring song — or a hard-won truth.
The sensation of a brilliant thought arriving; Archimedes' joyful cry from the bath, meaning 'I've got it!'.
The condition in which the deadline was yesterday and one has only just opened the laptop.
The noble art of putting important matters off until later — say, to scroll social media instead.
One of the seven deadly sins and, conveniently, the chief engine of progress — we owe it the remote control and food delivery.
The capricious lady who calls on artists and poets exclusively at three in the morning.
The part of the body on which sit those unable to solve their own problems.
The foliage beneath the nose, found on cats, hussars and Salvador Dali.
A polite Japanese honorific placed after a name.
The extremely poisonous tropical tree of Asia, named for the mythical guard of the underworld on account of its deadly fruit.
The edible cactus with flat, spined pads, depicted even on the coat of arms of Mexico.
The lush garden flower with enormous scented buds the size of a cabbage head, opening at the start of summer.
The profusely flowering shrub of the rhododendron family; in winter, on a windowsill, it becomes one continuous pink or red bouquet.
The longest river in Europe, running from the Valdai Hills to the Caspian — and the name of a Soviet saloon car with a deer on the bonnet.
The legendary Hollywood actor of The Godfather and Scarface, who made 'Hoo-ah!' his calling card.
